column2: Act Eight
The Big Brother
The Black King Nidhogg shall return.
He is despair, he is hell, and with wings hung with human bones he shall blot out the sky.
He is Skuld’s shears. On the day of his vengeance, even if you are Odin, when you leave your palace bearing your invincible spear, the road you take will be one from which there is no return.
Was this not the prophecy we have believed for the past hundred years?
“An egg…” Number 13 thought. “A brass egg.”
Was a report on this really worth five million dollars? Number 13 hesitated. It seemed unreal. Was the money really that easy to earn?

Inside the quartz-glass chamber stood a jar, made of brass and covered in dark green corrosion. Faint engraved designs in the Gandhara style showed two snakes guarding a great tree. Its outer wall had once been completely sealed, but a patch near the top had a gray-tin sheen, and a dark hole gaped there, apparently eaten through by corrosion.
All in all, it looked very much like an egg.

But there was no doubt that it was his target. The metallic smell of corrosion in the air had grown chokingly strong here, and the powerful magnetic field sent a loose little screw flying from his watch. It clung to the outer wall of the quartz chamber, trembling. No wonder the laboratory was made entirely of glass, with hardly a trace of metal in sight.
Dozens of pairs of eyes watched him from behind. If he kept staring at the target in a daze, sooner or later they would see through him.
Number 13 thought quickly. “What is this thing? What makes information about it worth five million dollars?”
Then it dawned on him. “Right! They don’t care about the shell. It’s what’s inside that matters!”
“No wonder the instructions said to look at it with my own eyes. No turning back now! I’ll take a peek inside!” Number 13 steeled himself.
In full view of everyone, he tore off his lab coat, sprang onto the console, and rose on tiptoe to peer through the opening.
The black hole was like a well of time.
“Brother, there are a lot of people outside.”
“We may die, I suppose. But don’t be afraid, Constantine.”
“I’m not afraid. As long as I’m with you, I’m not afraid… But why… won’t you eat me? If you ate me, there’s no prison you couldn’t break out of.”
“You would make fine food. But then I would be too lonely. For thousands of years, you’ve been the only one with me.”

“But dying really is so sad. It’s like being sealed inside a black box, forever and ever, pitch-black… Like feeling your way through the night, but no matter how far you reach, your hands never touch a thing…”

“The fate of the forsaken is to cross the wilderness, raise their battle banners once more, and return to their homeland. Death is nothing to fear. It is only a long sleep. Until I can devour this world, I would rather sleep in peace than wander alone. We will wake again.”
“Brother… when you raise the battle banners and devour the world, will you eat me?”
“Yes. And then you and I will reign over the world together!”
“Who’s… talking?” Number 13 felt dizzy.
It was as though he really stood beside a well, listening to people speaking below. Someone in the darkness at the bottom looked up at him.
The well was deep, and he could fall in at any moment.
“Damn it! Why is it always dialogue from some second-rate stage play?” Number 13 jerked his gaze away.

It felt a little like being bewitched. Something that old might well carry an evil presence. Fortunately, Number 13 had never cared about ghosts and supernatural nonsense. Even so, his heart was pounding.

“Lin, bing, dou, zhe, jie, zhen, lie, zai, qian!” Number 13 recited the words in terrible Chinese, pulled out his shotgun, and turned it on the dumbstruck researchers beyond the reinforced glass. “If you don’t mind dying, put your hands up!”
He had learned those nine words from cartoons. They were first-rate for warding off evil: words powerful enough to cut down any god or Buddha that stood in his way.
Number 13 let out a long breath. Whether the words had really worked or he was simply strong-minded, the lingering voices in his head faded away.

The principal froze for an instant, then promptly raised both hands. He seemed an old man sensible enough to recognize the situation. Disbelief was written in the researchers’ eyes, but they followed his lead and raised their hands too.
“That’ll do. I’ll add a line to the report saying I looked inside through the opening and saw nothing,” Number 13 thought. “Only it was almost as if… someone in there looked at me.”
But that was obviously impossible. At liquid-nitrogen temperatures, even a flagellate inside would have frozen to death.
“I’ll treat it like a report for a high-school field exercise. Good enough.” Number 13 kicked open the cryogenic-chamber door.
A researcher suddenly flipped up a clear plastic cover on the console and slapped the red button underneath.
“Dragon’s Den entering lockdown! Entering lockdown!” A stern female voice echoed through the air.
Behind Number 13, the reinforced outer cover around the quartz chamber snapped shut. Twelve sealing valves locked at once as a flood of liquid nitrogen poured into the quartz chamber.
“Are you calling the cops? Do you think I’m robbing a twenty-four-hour convenience store?” Number 13 was furious at this unexpected development.

He ought to have pressed his sawed-off shotgun to the researcher’s forehead and blown his head off. But the sight of blood made him a little faint, and every shell had been thoroughly soaked in the aquarium. So he stepped forward and kicked the man over, taking seven or eight other researchers down with him. In the confusion, Number 13 turned and sprinted from the lab.

Something clattered behind him. He looked back and saw a gray-tin bottle that had fallen from his pocket and was rolling across the floor. He had kicked too hard. It was one of the pieces of equipment his employer had sent before the operation, with instructions only to carry it; no one had explained its purpose. It looked like an antique. He hesitated for a brief second, decided there was no point going back for something so useless, and raced toward the end of the corridor.
“Stop him!” the principal shouted.
The researchers came to their senses and swarmed out after him.
At that moment, in the channel above the aquarium, the phone Number 13 had lost in an underwater crevice suddenly lit up.

“Number 13, if you are still alive at this point, you should be close to the target. Your target is a brass jar approximately 1.8 meters high and 1.2 meters in diameter, with a corroded opening at the top. Final instruction: open the gray-tin bottle and pour the solution through that opening. Once the mission is complete, your bonus will be raised to ten million dollars.”
At last water reached the battery, and the phone stopped working forever.

In the shadow of the cryogenic-chamber door, someone sighed softly. Everyone had rushed out in pursuit, and in the confusion no one noticed him. “So the mission failed just like that? Young people really are unreliable,” he said quietly.
He stepped out of the shadows, picked up the tin bottle Number 13 had left, walked to the quartz chamber, and inserted a black card into the slot on the console.

“This operation will open the Dragon’s Den. There is a possibility that Norton, King of Bronze and Fire, will awaken. Operation prohibited! Operation prohibited! Operation prohibited!” Norma’s voice rang through the laboratory. Buzzers blared, every warning light came on, and red light swept across the room.
“Be quiet, Norma. This is the moment we witness a miracle.” The man pulled down a manual lever, cutting off all communication between the laboratory and Norma.
The main power went out. Norma’s voice vanished, and the lights went dark one by one, leaving only the independently powered alarm buzzing and the warning lights revolving.
In the darkness flowed the crimson of the warning lights, crimson like magma, crimson like blood… the crimson of the end of the world.
It illuminated the man’s expressionless face.

The temperature rose rapidly. The stream of electrons rotating at high speed in the superconducting magnetic field weakened, and the quartz chamber suspended in midair slowly descended. The twelve sealing valves opened simultaneously, a great volume of white vapor burst out, and the reinforced outer cover, strong enough to withstand submachine-gun fire, swung open.

“I offer my bones and blood to the great sovereign Nidhogg, the supreme, the almighty, the all-virtuous, who rules the world through destiny.” The man reached out and touched the quartz chamber. He felt vibrations coming from within, growing stronger and stronger.
“Excellent. You haven’t kept me waiting too long!” He drew a knife from his sleeve and plunged it into the thick wall of the quartz chamber.

The blade cut into quartz glass as though it were jelly. He pulled the knife out, leaving a cut that glowed faint blue in the glass. The vacuum inside was broken, and air screamed in. With one stroke he sliced the neck from the gray-tin bottle and aimed the broken opening at the crack. The gray-tin liquid followed the cut into the chamber, moving like a slender snake around the inner wall, keeping away from the brass jar as though afraid of it. But as more liquid entered, the gray stream began to boil and bubble, crackling like something alive… cheering in anticipation of victory.
The man slipped the knife back into his sleeve and withdrew from the cryogenic lab.

At the door he looked back one last time. In an instant, all the gray-tin solution flew away from the inner wall and “pounced” on the brass jar. On contact, violent corrosion followed. The indestructible jar softened like cheese in a microwave, spraying dark green mist in every direction.
An indescribable low roar echoed through the cryogenic lab, frantic and seething.
“Welcome back to the world, Constantine.” The man closed the door.
“Damn it! Come on! One step closer and I’ll blow you away!” Number 13 waved his shotgun with a murderous look.

The elevator doors slowly opened behind him. The gun was pointed at the pale-faced researchers. They clearly had no combat experience: having chased him this far, they had bunched together into a perfect target.
“Does anyone have a useful Yanling? Think of something!” one researcher said.
“Our Yanling are all… research-oriented… Why else would we be in the Research Department?” someone replied dejectedly. “You think I don’t want to join the Executive Department?”

The lights suddenly went out. A moment later a piercing alarm rolled through the dark corridor, ten times more grating than before. The white light from the elevator illuminated the researchers’ faces, now even paler.
“The cryogenic lab!” someone said.
“We didn’t leave anyone there! Oh, God!”

The researchers ran back as though mad, paying no attention to the shotgun aimed at them. Apparently the thing was more important to them than their lives. Number 13 was left standing bewildered before the elevator, suddenly feeling unimportant—and a little disappointed by it.
“What’s going on? I have to say, your power distribution system is really terrible,” Number 13 muttered.

He smashed the elevator buttons with the butt of his gun, destroying them all, then stepped backward into the elevator. The doors closed and he breathed a sigh of relief. Only two emergency elevators went directly from here to the ground floor. With the buttons destroyed, nobody could follow him.

“So that counts as… success?” Number 13 fixed his hair in the mirror-bright elevator doors. But something was wrong. It felt as though a hand had gripped his heart; his blood seemed to be racing faster, and breathing was growing harder.
Why was the pressure so intense? It was as though something had come after him… when the darkness fell!
A metallic hiss!
Amid a tidal roar, metal rang out.
“She… drew her swords!” Caesar suddenly understood.

He tossed both Desert Eagles into the air, swept his coat aside, and drew Dictator from behind his waist, slashing an extraordinarily swift cross. Three blades clashed in the dark. In the flying sparks, Caesar caught a fleeting glimpse of Mai Sakatoku’s pointed face, the crimson shadow at the corners of her eyes vivid as blood.
At the last instant, Caesar had guessed right. The duel Mai intended was not with guns. She had drawn her swords.

Mai Sakatoku wore two Glocks in conspicuous holsters. A member of the Mint club, proud of her looks, figure, and passion, she appeared every inch a fashionable woman. Yet the weapons she truly favored were those two antique-looking swords.
She specialized in close combat.

It had been a matter of an instant. If the two Desert Eagles had not slowed Mai slightly, Caesar would already have been struck head-on. A sword fight was different from a gunfight. The guns fired Frigga rounds, but this was a fight to the death.
Mai withdrew as soon as their blades touched.
Caesar lowered his head and listened with all his attention.
But he could not find her. Somehow Mai had slowed her heartbeat drastically and masked it with the whistling.

Nor could he easily detect the sound of her swords in advance. The two blades were specially designed to meet minimal air resistance and make almost no sound; what little sound they made was identical to the whistle of the butterfly hair clips at her temples.
Two intertwined whistles whirled rapidly around Caesar, now high, now low, now ahead, now behind, like ghosts.
Mai had yet to strike a second time. But from what angle would the next blow come? He could not imagine.
“Are all Japanese people ninjas?” Caesar asked. “Whistling and high-speed movement make me lose track of you. Interesting.”
“Are all Italian men so pretentious?” Her voice came from directly ahead, but the whistling was behind him.
“Let’s make this quick. Three strikes. Can you kill me?” Caesar asked.
“All right, three. But don’t be afraid. At worst you’ll be badly injured and crippled. I’ve always gone easy on men whose figures match mine.”
“I also maintain a gentleman’s manners with ladies who have good figures!”

His blade lowered, Caesar abandoned every defensive posture and stood motionless. His concentration, however, rose to its peak. Invisible commands went out, his domain expanded, and the Kamaitachi danced wildly through the void.
“First strike!” He caught the sound of her soft laughter a meter directly in front of him.

Caesar abruptly raised his hand. Dictator did not slash ahead but blocked above his head. A fraction of a second later he caught the whistling and the sound of a blade overhead. The real blow came straight down at the crown of his head. The swords clashed, and Mai, light as a cicada’s wing, used the force of the impact to glide silently away, vanishing into the dark again.
“I’m amazed how sharp your Kamaitachi is in your hands, third-year.” Mai’s laughter came from everywhere.
“That was only the beginning. You’ve sped up again.” Caesar returned to his position, head lowered, standing silently. “Speed against sensitivity?”
“That’s right. Second strike!”

Caesar stiffened. Whistling and blade sounds came simultaneously from overhead and underfoot; there seemed to be two Mais, one above and one below. He dove forward, sweeping Dictator horizontally behind him to form a defensive screen. The straight blade pursuing him passed less than a centimeter from Dictator without making a sound, and Mai vanished into the darkness again.
“You used the sound of your hair clips to create an imaginary double.” Caesar rolled across the floor and got to his feet.
“Clever. Third strike—and the last!”

Caesar breathed deeply, drawing each breath to the bottom of his lungs. He had to concentrate, give everything he had. This was a rare opportunity for real combat. He had never faced an opponent like this. Sweat poured from every pore, soaking his shirt as though he had just run a marathon on the track. Yet he felt exhilarated. Every Kamaitachi had awakened, shrieking with excitement.
He had absolute confidence. Fighting at his side was an army of wind demons!
He heard the sound of a bamboo flute splitting and suddenly froze.
The wind through the butterfly clips at Mai’s temples had sounded like a mournful Japanese flute. Now the notes were fading, leaving only a faint, indistinct echo.
There was only one explanation. Mai, whose advantage was extreme speed, had suddenly stopped, abandoning everything she had in her favor.
Strangely, the last echo came from every direction, all 360 degrees. A Mai stood at every degree around him.
In a world with light, that would have been impossible. No Yanling could produce anything like the art of making doubles.
But in a world of utter darkness, judging from the sounds the Kamaitachi had gathered, that was precisely what had happened.
Caesar kept his head lowered. In his mind, countless Mais stood in a circle around him, raising their swords very, very slowly so the blades would make no sound.
Three hundred and sixty sharp blades, ready to strike at any moment.
Caesar smiled silently. With that smile, his spirit collapsed, his domain contracted in an instant, and the Kamaitachi flew back, like countless crows returning to their nests in the dark.
He had abandoned his own advantage too.
The final strike was like a duel between samurai of old. The killing intent had frozen time itself; all that remained was for a falling leaf to break the silence and send blades flashing forth.
Ding!

The sound, like a bell, cut in like a blade and severed the taut string. The balance shattered. Three hundred and sixty Mais rushed in at once, a blade at every degree of the circle. Mai Sakatoku’s Blade-Whirlwind Storm closed around him in a gale of flashing steel.
Caesar spun, crouched, gripped his blade in both hands, and slashed with all his strength toward his right rear!
In that last instant he no longer tried to judge where his enemy was. The force and angle of his stroke had already been fixed in his mind, as precisely as though measured with a square.

Dictator met one of the 360 Mais. The blades scraped with a piercing sound. All the other illusions collapsed at that instant. Their breath struck each other’s faces, all their strength pressing against the steel.
“Not bad. How did you find my real position?” Mai asked.
“How did you make sounds in every direction at once?” Caesar countered.
“Shouldn’t a gracious Italian man be the first to reveal his tactical secret?”

“Your heartbeat. You studied ninjutsu and suppressed its sound, but as you moved at high speed, your heartbeat quickened involuntarily. At the end, the sound of the butterflies was no longer enough to cover it. That’s why I agreed on three strikes. During the first two, your heartbeat was still hard to pick up.”
“My mistake… I thought Italian men had no brains for anything but chasing women…” In the dark, Mai pouted.
“Your turn,” Caesar said.
“The winner doesn’t need to say much,” Mai said.
Something cold pressed against Caesar’s forehead. He froze, then realized it was Mai’s Glock.

One hand held her sword against Dictator; the other held the gun to his forehead. “Put the knife down. I don’t know what happens if a Frigga round is fired against your forehead. Maybe it won’t have time to vaporize and will just punch a hole through your skull?”
“Hey… we agreed to use blades.” Resigned, Caesar relaxed the pressure on his knife.
“When did I ever say that? Even if I did, you believed a girl who said it?” Mai slapped his forehead. “With emotional intelligence that low, you’ll never find a girlfriend, will you?”
“I thought Japanese people followed bushido,” Caesar said. “And I do have a girlfriend.”

Caesar’s grandfather had once told him how inflexible Japanese bushido was. On the Sino-Japanese battlefield, he said, when Japanese and Chinese soldiers fought with bayonets, the Japanese always unloaded their rifles according to the infantry manual, whereas the Chinese fought with their guns loaded. When the two sides locked blades, the Chinese soldier pulled the trigger… bang… oh dear. Then he turned to fight the next Japanese soldier.
“It was because of allies like that that Italy lost the Second World War!” Caesar’s grandfather concluded.
“The Japan you know is the one from the Meiji Restoration in 1868, isn’t it?” Mai curled her lip.
“Brother.” The childish voice seemed to rise from a deep well.
A scorching wind struck their faces. Brilliant light hurt their eyes through their closed lids, and their noses filled with the heavy smell of burning.

Both threw themselves down at once. For an instant something had pressed on them so hard their hearts nearly stopped, a pressure a hundred times stronger than Blade-Whirlwind Storm, so terrifying they could barely breathe.
The pressure vanished in a flash, but during that brief instant they had felt as though they were in a blazing hell.
“What… happened?” they asked together.
“I don’t know,” they answered together.

Both opened their eyes. The hall should have been pitch-black, but now a faint light flickered there. It seemed to have been swept by a wind of fire. Thick smoke hung everywhere, and rows of oak benches had been broken in two at the middle, their jagged ends glowing dark red. The old, hard oak was slowly burning, though no one knew what had ignited it. After so many years, the wood was nearly as hard as cast iron.
“Tell your college secretary to turn on the lights!” Mai ordered.
“An intermission, right? We haven’t called a truce,” Caesar said.
“I have the advantage, so I’ll give you a break, third-year.” Mai withdrew her Glock.
“Norma, lights on!” Caesar slowly put Dictator away.
There was no response. The hall remained dark.
“Norma isn’t answering. I don’t know why.” Caesar tried to stay calm. As an A-rank student, he had authorization with Norma; never before had she failed to respond.
“Did a breaker trip?” Mai was growing irritated. “What third-rate company installed your power system at Cassell College?”
“It’s all right. I have a jet lighter for cigars… It gives a decent flame.” Caesar took a lighter in a solid silver case from his pocket.
“Get out of the way! What use are you?” Impatient, Mai pulled a flare from the back pocket of her combat suit.

The flare lit the area. Their comrades, unconscious from Frigga rounds, still lay quietly where they had fallen. Apart from the oak benches being displaced and burning, there seemed to be nothing else amiss.
“So you had that many butterflies,” Caesar said.

Around them, eight silver butterfly hair clips hung on threads as fine as spider silk. Mai had used them to create the illusion of doubles in every direction. She took down the butterflies and put them away. When Caesar reached for one to examine it, she glared until he withdrew his hand.
“Don’t go collecting women’s things for no reason!”
Caesar shook his head helplessly.
“There are holes in the floor of the dais,” Mai said.

Caesar followed her pointing finger. Hole after hole formed two rows across the dais floor, like… a trail of footprints. But each footprint had burned all the way through the teak boards, exposing the gray concrete underneath.
Caesar put his own foot over the prints to compare them. “If a person made these, they’d be about one meter sixty tall. The stride is only two-thirds of mine.”
Mai tried them too. “Even though I’m ten centimeters shorter than you, his stride is only two-thirds of mine too… Oh, I didn’t mean your legs are short… Third-year, follow the tracks.”
“Stop calling me third-year! Caesar. Caesar Gattuso. You should show even an enemy basic respect!”
“I’ll change what I call you when you make fourth year.” Mai followed the footprints behind the statue of Odin.
They drew deep breaths and looked at each other, their hearts pounding with apprehension.
“Do you hide something strange at this college of yours?” Mai asked.
“There are plenty of strange things here, but none that strange,” Caesar said. “You didn’t bring it?”
Mai shook her head. “No idea at all.”
“To melt through a metal door this thick would take hours even with a welding torch, wouldn’t it?” Caesar crouched beside it.
“The technique was very practiced. The proportions of the human figure are too precise,” Mai said.

They both understood what the earlier ding had been: the elevator arriving. Perhaps because communications with Norma had been cut, the doors had not opened. But there was a hole in them, clearly melted through. Its edges glowed dazzlingly; steel had melted to red-hot liquid and dripped onto the floor.
One look made it obvious that the hole was… human-shaped!
“Came up in the elevator from the underground level?” Mai looked at Caesar. “To melt an alloy like this, his temperature would have to be roughly the same as the surface of the sun…”

“There’s something else I can’t explain,” Caesar said quietly. “Before I recalled Kamaitachi, this person was already nearly here. My mind was entirely focused on heartbeats then, but I picked up no unfamiliar one… If he’s a person, his heart isn’t beating.”
Cold sweat soaked Mai’s underwear. She was silent for a long time. “Third-year, stand away from me. I need to make a call.”
At the college gate, several students stood guard with guns. By the time they heard the roar of a motorcycle, it was already too late.

A dazzling streak of silver raced toward them at tremendous speed. It was a Harley, swerving in a perilous arc to dodge the spray of bullets and slice past them. Some said the Mongols were a people born in the saddle; this man must have come from a people born on motorcycle seats.
“Hallelujah! God always favors handsome men!” Number 13 shouted.

It had gone so smoothly. After leaving the underground levels, he had quickly found a silver Harley, the kind of beautiful machine he had dreamed of owning. Best of all, the key was still in the ignition.

This accident-filled mission was finally over. Now he would go collect his five million dollars, retire, and spend the rest of his life roaming the world in shameless style, touring Pacific islands of white sand, blue seas, and endless shapely legs! Overflowing with joy, Number 13 looked back and made a face. In the darkness behind him, girls still wearing white formal dresses held their high heels in one hand and sprayed Uzi fire with the other, but clearly they could no longer catch him.
Suddenly dazzling lights swept over him from the side, accompanied by the surging roar of an engine.
“An ambush?” Number 13 was horrified.
It was too late to swerve. He jumped from the motorcycle, relying on his excellent leaping ability, and rolled several times upon landing, swallowing a mouthful of dust before coming to a stop.
The Harley flew over the car roof in a streak of silver, struck a roadside guard stone, and sailed off the cliff.

Lu Mingfei watched the silver streak in alarm, then the man rolling across the road ahead. “Oh no… The first time I drive a car this expensive and I have an accident… Senior, it really wasn’t my fault… Riding a motorcycle in the middle of the night is one thing, but why didn’t he even turn on his lights?”

He had no American driver’s license and felt terribly uneasy. He jumped out of the car, went over to the other party, and rubbed his hands together. “Are you hurt…? I… you came out so suddenly,” he said in less-than-fluent English.
“Hey… what are you doing?” Lu Mingfei’s hands shot up.
A black gun barrel pressed upward beneath his chin. Number 13 looked furious.
“Stop him! He’s an intruder!” the pursuing students shouted behind them.
“Were you lying in wait for me?” Number 13 demanded viciously.
“I have nothing to do with them! Absolutely nothing! I was just driving past to buy a hot dog.” Lu Mingfei knew how to read a situation.
He had no idea whether he could fool this “dragon,” but its appearance was far from what he had expected.

If the dragon had a blue-green face, two horns, and catfish whiskers at the corners of its mouth, Lu Mingfei could have understood. But this man looked perfectly ordinary, a standard human being just like Lu Mingfei. He had a cheerful face, Chinese-style black hair, and a pair of distinctively drooping eyebrows… Strange. Why did those eyebrows look so familiar?
Lu Mingfei’s pupils widened. “Hey… aren’t you Old Tang?”
Number 13 froze. “That cheeky face of yours… You look a lot like Big-Headed Bear…”

Lu Mingfei used a picture of a big-headed bear as his avatar in their StarCraft group. Apart from classmates and professors like Nono and Fingel, Old Tang was his only friend in America. On countless nights they had bombarded each other across StarCraft maps. During Lu Mingfei’s Cassell College interview, Old Tang had even video-called him and helped him correct his spoken English. Because he knew Old Tang, Lu Mingfei felt there was at least one familiar place on the map of America: Brooklyn, New York.

How could he run into Old Tang here? And how had he ended up with Old Tang holding a gun on him? Wasn’t Old Tang supposed to be in Brooklyn living on welfare? Hadn’t he said he would take him around America on a Greyhound? The world turned upside down inside Lu Mingfei’s head.
“Someone you know?” Nono had both hands raised in the car beside them.
“Old Tang… I’m Big-Headed Bear… No, I’m Mingming… Don’t shoot… What are you doing here?” Lu Mingfei looked ready to cry. Mingming was his ID in the group.

“We’ll talk in the group later! In the group later! I just came to do a little job… Now it’s done and I’m in a hurry to leave, but they won’t let me…” Old Tang looked past Lu Mingfei’s shoulder at the Bugatti Veyron, then gave Nono an appraising look. “Mm! Hot girl! Lend me the car, will you?”
“You’ve already borrowed my boyfriend’s Harley,” Nono said. At the instant of the collision, she had recognized the motorcycle flying overhead as Caesar’s favorite.

Old Tang looked Lu Mingfei up and down. “I underestimated you. Who’d have thought you’d latch onto a pretty girl as soon as you got abroad? She’s got a Bugatti Veyron and a Harley! What kind of world is this?”
“I was about to ask the same thing!” Lu Mingfei held his hands high. “You can borrow the car. No need to give it back!”
“I’ll need to borrow you and your hot girl as hostages too!” Old Tang dragged Lu Mingfei into the Bugatti.
“Drive!” he shouted at Nono.
“Old Tang, what do you want? Can’t you show a little consideration for an old friend?” Lu Mingfei shouted.
“Shut up! I’m putting on a show. I’ll let you go once we’re down the mountain,” Old Tang whispered. Then he roared at their approaching pursuers, “Come any closer and I’ll kill him!”

He did his best to look ferocious. His cheerful face was sometimes a curse; people often thought he was joking instead of threatening them. But this time his menace seemed to work. The Gothic girls in white dresses, guns in hand, suddenly stopped. Their expressions froze, and they backed away step by step.
“Hey, what’s with those faces? Is that… the look people get when they see a ghost?” Old Tang was surprised.
The effect was good, but a little too good.
Then he felt a hot wind sweeping in behind him, as though a sun were rising there. Trembling, he turned toward Nono. Her long hair streamed wildly forward in the hot wind.
All three found themselves unable to breathe. The girls were afraid not of Old Tang but of some… thing standing behind them.
The enormous pressure threatened to crush them.
Old Tang did not dare turn around. It was as though a wolf stood behind him, ready to tear out his throat if he looked back. He poked Lu Mingfei in the waist. “You look.”
“Don’t be stupid. You’re such a hero, so why don’t you look instead of telling me to?” Lu Mingfei trembled.
“Don’t turn around,” Nono said, her voice shaking. “Look in the rearview mirror.”
In the mirror, a burning figure stood on the engine cover at the rear of the Bugatti. Arms spread, he slowly bent down, as though about to embrace and kiss either Old Tang or Lu Mingfei.

His face grew clearer in the mirror. His pupils burned with brilliant gold, and his face seemed cracked like the earth, lava flowing in the fissures. On that horrifying face, a horrifying expression slowly blossomed.
“Brother,” he said softly.
“Ghost!” Lu Mingfei and Old Tang clung to each other and screamed, their mouths wide enough to fit a pineapple.
“Everyone, take cover! Everyone, take cover!” Professor Schneider’s roar echoed over the campus loudspeakers.

As the shout rang out, the burning figure passed a high-voltage transformer. Its metal casing melted instantly, and brilliant sparks erupted like a fountain to a man’s height. Then the explosion scorched the surrounding lawn to black earth.

Gunfire thundered. Dense streams of bullets converged from both sides as students trained for the battlefield took cover behind buildings on either side of the lawn and laid down a perfect crossfire. Both groups carried standard M4-series weapons, firing 5.56-millimeter steel-core rounds at nine hundred rounds a minute. They emptied magazines in an instant and immediately replaced them to keep firing. After the failure of the earlier volleys, the person in charge this time was holding nothing back. Lancelot, the Lionheart Society’s vice president and a third-year student from France, directed the assault.

Not a single bullet hit the figure. About two meters from him, they melted, as though an invisible dark fire formed a barrier there. Red-hot molten steel coursed at high speed over its surface, gathering in ever greater quantities. The bullets struck it in vain, like moths hurling themselves into a flame.

With muffled reports, dozens of smoke trails sped toward the figure. The students were using forty-millimeter rifle grenades fitted to the M4 series, powerful enough on a direct hit to destroy an infantry fighting vehicle.
The figure did not move, but the molten steel whirling around him did. It sprayed outward and caught every grenade in midair, sending the force of the explosions entirely away from him.
Firelight illuminated Lancelot’s face, which twitched slightly.
“President, bullets and rifle grenades are useless against him.” He held a phone to his ear.
In the ruined chapel, Chu Zihang and his opponent faced each other across a great distance. Despite trading attacks with Yanling: Sovereign Flame, both had somehow kept their clothes intact.
“Lancelot, retreat! If he can command metal and fire, he belongs to the line of Norton, King of Bronze and Fire. Retreat before he uses Sovereign Flame!”
Chu Zihang hung up.
“Is this your plan?” he asked.

“If this were our plan, I wouldn’t have given you time to make a phone call.” The three-nothings girl’s voice was as calm as ever. After meeting Chu Zihang’s high-risk Yanling with her own, she did not even need to catch her breath. “An accident? I believe you,” Chu Zihang said.
“You believe me?”
“Unlike Caesar, I know what the ‘three nothings’ really mean: no words, no heart, no expression. You’re the kind of person with no heart, too lazy to lie.”
“Then we’ll settle this next time.” The three-nothings girl turned and left.
“I look forward to it.”
A low chant echoed over the lawn. The smell of burning grew stronger in the air, and above the figure’s head the air seemed to catch fire.
A power beyond human understanding condensed there, and everyone felt its pressure.
“Everyone, take cover!” Schneider and Lancelot shouted at once.
The power shattered.
Like a napalm bomb bursting in the air, flames surged from a single point in every direction, carrying a powerful shock wave.
The nearest building stood dozens of meters from the figure, yet all the glass around him shattered. Flames shot through the windows, like tongues of fire breathed inside by an enormous dragon.

When the explosion ended, every blade of grass around the figure had burned away, leaving the ground black. The figure stood at the center of what looked like a black sun emblem and began to chant again!
“That’s… Sovereign Flame?” Lancelot murmured.
He suddenly realized he had never truly understood Chu Zihang’s potential and bloodline. They inspired not merely admiration, but something stronger… fear!
The library control room.
“Dad! Can you activate Edict now?” Manstein roared into the phone. “That dragon… it should be a dragon… is setting off high-risk Yanling all over campus!”
“Don’t be ridiculous. Edict can’t affect a bloodline of a higher order than mine! That dragon…” The old cowboy’s voice shook too. “It appears to be a first-generation dragon!”
“First-generation… Aren’t those… the Four Monarchs?” Sweat streamed down Manstein’s face.
Schneider gripped the microphone, his expression grim. He said nothing. He was out of options and did not know what instructions to give more than a thousand students on campus.
“Where the hell have you been?” Mai finally got through on the phone.
She had been stamping her feet in Valhalla for ten minutes, and the other party had not answered once.
“Mai, aren’t you finished yet? Looks like that Caesar Gattuso gave you trouble.” The other woman spoke lazily, her voice indistinct, as though she were chewing something crisp.

“Stop eating chips! Everything here is a mess! A shadow covered in flames is setting fire to everything, erupting like a steel furnace about to explode. This place will be flattened soon!” Mai shouted furiously. “Was this part of your plan? Next time, could you stop squeezing out your plans bit by bit like toothpaste? Tell me everything!”
“A man like a steel furnace?” The chewing stopped abruptly. One could almost imagine a chip falling from that lazy mouth.
“Impossible! Absolutely impossible!” the woman on the phone cried.
Caesar snatched the phone from Mai’s hand. “I can confirm it. Exactly as Miss Sakatoku says, the man like a steel furnace is now less than a hundred meters away from us.”
“Who are you?”
“Caesar Gattuso, third year at Cassell College.” Caesar handed the phone back to Mai.
“Hey, Mai! You must have made a mistake. Weren’t you and that guy supposed to be fighting to the death?” the woman said.

“We can fight to the death later! At this rate we’ll all be dead! I can’t even get out now!” Mai watched a ball of fire blossom on the nearby lawn. “He’s evolved from a steel furnace into a fire-breathing dragon!”
She dropped into a crouch. Flames shot through the window above her head, a two-meter serpent of fire flashing into being and vanishing.
“Take a video on your phone and send it to me!” the woman said anxiously.
“Chips Girl, sometimes you’re impossibly fussy!” Mai cursed her, but raised the phone to the window and began recording.

The high-speed 3G network carried her signal swiftly to Chicago. Their support there was stunned and leaped out of the water in a panic. “Damn it! That isn’t Norton in his normal state at all… It’s… Constantine gone berserk! Did you do something to set him off?”
“I don’t know! I know absolutely nothing about dragon nervous systems! Think of something, fast!” Mai exploded. “Is your plan to get every one of us killed here?”
“Of course not. Norton was supposed to appear in his normal state!”
“But now he’s slaughtering everything in his path! As they say, he’ll kill any man or god who gets in his way!”
“Hey, are you still there?” Mai shouted. Suddenly there was no sound on the other end.

“I’m here!” The woman’s voice betrayed desperate urgency, rare for someone who usually maneuvered so effortlessly. “I’m accessing databases overseas, looking for information on an out-of-control Dragon King. This is an extreme situation! Extremely rare! I didn’t expect it at all, and I’m completely unprepared!”
“What exactly is an out-of-control Dragon King?”

“One awakened by the wrong person, in the wrong way. His powers haven’t stabilized and his body hasn’t fully developed. He looks amazingly powerful because he can’t control that power, but his body won’t be able to withstand it. He could collapse at any moment!”
“What happens if he collapses?”
“What happens when the King of Bronze and Fire collapses? Yanling: Torch Dragon, of course! The only question is how large the blast radius will be.”
“How large?”
“I don’t know, but I’m sure it will flatten the college.”
“Then… hurry up! Think of something! Aren’t you always so quick?”
“I was taking a bubble bath.”
“What does your bubble bath have to do with it?” Mai paused.

“So my communications equipment is all in the hotel safe. I can only use the laptop I have with me to get online and try to connect to the core server… Damn it! The network says I have to pay twenty-five dollars a night for internet service and enter the last four digits of my credit card… Wait, I have to find my card… First I need to wrap myself in a bath towel!”
“You always book those lousy hotels! Call me back quickly!” Furious, Mai hung up.
A few minutes later, the door of a room in a Chicago hotel was kicked open.

A middle-aged man kissing his wife on the sofa stared at the woman who burst in. She was a woman capable of shaking a man’s resolve, making her entrance in a pose capable of shaking it. She wore only a pink bathrobe, her wet hair wrapped in a towel; she was obviously naked underneath, and two long, slender legs were exposed… In one hand she held a laptop, in the other a stack of American bills.

“I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to interrupt, but I really can’t find my credit card, so I had to come in and ask to borrow your internet connection,” the woman said. “You’ve activated the internet service, haven’t you?”
“Y-yes.” The man nodded.
“This money is compensation.” The woman threw the cash on the bed and hurried to the desk to connect the network cable. “You can carry on with whatever you were doing. Just pretend I’m not here.”
“Old Tang, where did you get a bugged unit like that?” Lu Mingfei was already calm, because he had no tears left to cry.

He had barely spent a few pleasant days admiring beautiful girls in the luxurious classrooms and library after joining the college when one deadly incident followed another. This time it really did not look like a game.
“I really didn’t create it.” Old Tang swallowed. “You know my tactical style has always been cautious. If I’d known it was this dangerous, would I have come?”
“Could you two stop talking in StarCraft language at a time like this?” Nono said.

The three stood shoulder to shoulder in the narrow passage where Lu Mingfei had dodged bullets on Freedom Day, less than fifty meters from the man constantly erupting in flames. Scorching fire might flash past the passage entrance at any moment. Dangerous as it was, it seemed a place hidden in plain sight, making it hard for the ghostlike dragon to find them. If they appeared in his line of sight, he would pursue them relentlessly.

They were still alive thanks to Nono’s nerve. At the college gate she had slammed down the Bugatti’s accelerator. The supercar reached a hundred kilometers an hour in three seconds and charged into campus, throwing the dragon off. At the time, Old Tang and Lu Mingfei still thought everything they had seen was an illusion. Only when they turned to see two melted footprints in the Bugatti’s aluminum engine cover, then looked back to see the figure they had thrown off running after them, did they have to accept reality.
“What do we do?” Lu Mingfei said. “We can’t hide here forever. I keep feeling… as if he can smell us.”
“Rubbish! What smell? You smell like sashimi!” Old Tang said. “We absolutely can’t go out! We’ll die if we do!”
“But why do I feel… that he’s getting closer?” Nono said.
“Where does the other end lead?” Lu Mingfei whispered to her.
“Open ground, without any cover. Do you want to be attacked with napalm out in the open?” someone said in the dark.
Only then did the three realize there was a fourth person in the passage.
Nono reached into the darkness, grabbed the person by the collar, and pressed her fingers against his throat so he dared not struggle, then dragged him out.
“Senior, that move was so cool… Fingel, you dog, why is it you?” Lu Mingfei stared wide-eyed.
The person she had pulled out was his useless senior Fingel. The man was actually wearing pajamas, carrying a plastic bag, and in his mouth he still had…

“Damn it, man, why are you here with a chicken leg in your mouth? What use are you, you good-for-nothing? Caesar or Chu Zihang, either one showing up here would be better!” If Lu Mingfei could have raised his legs high enough, he would have liked to kick Fingel in the face a couple of times.
“Mmm mmm mmm mmm…” Fingel said.
“Do you think you’re a rooster?”

“I’m saying I-I-I-I-I… I only ordered a late-night snack from the dining hall, but they said they weren’t delivering tonight because of the alert… They didn’t forbid students from picking up their own orders, though, so I came out…” Fingel took the chicken leg out of his mouth, looking ready to cry.
“Think of something, quick! I think he… really is coming closer!” Old Tang whispered.

Footsteps sounded outside the passage, and it grew brighter and brighter, as though someone carrying a great lamp were approaching step by step in the middle of the night. All four fell silent, drenched in cold sweat.
Lu Mingfei’s premonition seemed right. The dragon could apparently smell them, sensing their position even without seeing them.
“We can’t go on running, can we? Every escape route leads to death. Wherever we hide, he’ll catch up in a few minutes,” Nono said softly.

“Calm down! Calm down!” Fingel said. “That thing is a dragon, right? A dragon on fire. No problem. If he’s on fire, we go somewhere with water. The pool! We’ll go to the pool in the gym! Water is the greatest weakness of fire-type Yanling. If we can suppress his power temporarily, maybe we can shoot him dead? The shortest way is through Valhalla. I’ve got a PPK too, modified. A good gun that can take down a dragon.” Fingel pulled a PPK from the waistband of his pajamas. It looked exactly like the aircraft-cannon version Masashi Toyama had demonstrated.
“Why bring a PPK to get a late-night snack? Can we rely on it?” Lu Mingfei asked.
“For self-defense… In theory, yes. Water overcomes fire. I got an A in advanced Yanling studies.”
“If there’s no other way, let’s run!” Nono shouted.

All four sprang up at once and raced toward the other end of the passage. The approaching footsteps behind them instantly quickened, and the light blazed as though a car with its headlights on were chasing them.
Someone kicked open the doors of Valhalla, and the four ran in like beaten dogs. At first sight of Caesar and Mai Sakatoku by the window, they all froze.
“Number 13?” Mai said. “You’re still alive? Where did you get lost?”
